narration.text: Welcome to the section on occupant protection and vehicle control. This first lesson covers seat belts. The guide states that wearing a seat belt correctly is the single most effective way to protect yourself, and that it sharply cuts your risk of a fatal injury in a crash. In this lesson you will learn the Washington seat belt law, where the shoulder belt and lap belt should sit, and the fit checks for the belt and your seating position. To remember: why seat belts matter; the seat belt law; how the belt should fit.

lines.text: All occupants of a moving vehicle.
Fastened belt or approved child restraint.

narration.text: Washington law covers everyone in the vehicle. All occupants of a moving vehicle need a fastened seat belt or an approved child restraint. Driving or riding without one is illegal. So the rule applies to the driver, the front-seat passenger and every passenger in the back. Children ride in an approved child restraint, which the next lesson covers in detail. Everyone else wears a fastened seat belt whenever the vehicle is moving. To remember: all occupants of a moving vehicle; fastened belt or approved child restraint; riding without one is illegal.

lines.text: Shoulder belt: across mid-chest and shoulder.
Never behind you, under your arm, on your neck.
Lap belt: snug on the hips below the stomach.

narration.text: The guide describes where each part of the belt goes. The shoulder belt goes snugly across the middle of the chest and shoulder. It never goes behind your back, under your arm, or across your neck or face. The lap belt holds the hips snugly below the stomach. So the shoulder belt crosses the chest, and the lap belt sits low on the hips. Both parts are snug, and neither is moved out of position for comfort. To remember: shoulder belt: across mid-chest and shoulder; never behind you, under your arm, on your neck; lap belt: snug on the hips below the stomach.

lines.text: Trap: belt behind the back for comfort.
Lap belt stays below the stomach.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some riders move the shoulder belt behind their back or under their arm, or let the lap belt ride up over the stomach. The guide rules these out. The shoulder belt goes snugly across the middle of the chest and shoulder, never behind your back, under your arm, or across the neck or face. The lap belt holds the hips snugly below the stomach. The correct position is the only one the guide describes. To remember: shoulder belt crosses mid-chest; lap belt stays below the stomach. A helpful hook for this lesson: ears, thighs, mid-shoulder.

lines.text: A back-seat passenger skips the belt.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a passenger in the back seat says seat belts are only for people in the front. What does Washington law say? Decide before the answer. The law is not limited to the front seat. The answer is that all occupants of a moving vehicle need a fastened seat belt or an approved child restraint. Driving or riding without one is illegal, so the back-seat passenger must buckle up too. A helpful hook for this lesson: ears, thighs, mid-shoulder. In short: under Washington law all occupants of a moving vehicle need a fastened seat belt or an approved child restraint, and riding without one is illegal.

lines.text: Untwisted; thighs; mid-shoulder; headrest at ears.

narration.text: To wrap up, wearing a seat belt correctly is the single most effective way to protect yourself in a crash. All occupants of a moving vehicle need a fastened seat belt or an approved child restraint. The shoulder belt crosses the middle of the chest and shoulder, and the lap belt holds the hips below the stomach. Check that the belt is not twisted, the lap portion sits on the upper thighs, the cross strap falls over mid-shoulder, and the headrest is in line with your ears. To remember: belt worn correctly: best protection; every occupant belted or restrained; untwisted; thighs; mid-shoulder; headrest at ears.

why_how.text: Children stay in each restraint stage as long as the seat allows, moving from rear-facing to harnessed to booster seats.
Airbags work together with seat belts, and children under thirteen should never ride in the front seat.

result.text: Maya rides in a harnessed car seat, facing either rearward or forward.

narration.text: This lesson covers how children ride safely. The guide sets standards for child restraints, explains who can check an installation, and lays out each restraint stage by age and height. It also covers airbags, which work together with seat belts, and the age below which children should never ride in the front seat. The stages have clear boundaries, and this lesson places each age and height on the right stage. To remember: restraint standards and installation; stages by age and height; airbags and the front seat. A helpful hook for this lesson: rear to two, harness to four, booster until the belt fits.

lines.text: Meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards.
Follow vehicle and seat makers' instructions.
A certified technician can check it.

narration.text: Child restraints must meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards. They must be installed following both the vehicle maker's instructions and the seat maker's instructions. A certified child passenger safety technician can check the installation. The guide also says to keep a child in each restraint stage as long as that seat allows. So a child does not move up to the next stage early; they stay in the current seat for as long as it fits them. To remember: meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards; follow vehicle and seat makers' instructions; A certified technician can check it.

lines.text: Birth until two: rear-facing car seat.
Two to four: harnessed car seat.
Harnessed seat may face either way.

narration.text: A child from birth until age two must use a car seat that faces the rear. Children aged two to four must ride in a car seat with a harness, which may face either rearward or forward. So the first stage is rear-facing only, and the second stage adds a harness requirement but allows either direction. Children aged two to four ride in a harnessed car seat, and from age four they move to a car or booster seat until the adult belt fits. To remember: birth until two: rear-facing car seat; two to four: harnessed car seat; harnessed seat may face either way.

lines.text: Car or booster seat until belts fit.
Usually between ages eight and twelve.
Booster: age four to four feet nine.

narration.text: Children aged four and older stay in a car or booster seat until the vehicle's lap and shoulder belts fit properly, usually between ages eight and twelve. The booster stage covers kids from four years old up to a height of four feet nine inches. Anyone taller than four feet nine inches who is old enough for a seat belt must wear a properly fitting belt. So leaving the booster depends on belt fit and height, not on a single birthday. To remember: car or booster seat until belts fit; usually between ages eight and twelve; booster: age four to four feet nine.

lines.text: Trap: one birthday ends the booster.
Booster exit: belt fit and height.
Front seat: separate line, under thirteen.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The child restraint rules use several numbers, and they answer different questions. Leaving the booster depends on belt fit and a height over four feet nine inches, typically between ages eight and twelve. The front-seat rule is a separate age line of under thirteen. So a child who has left the booster may still be under thirteen, and children under thirteen should never ride in the front seat. Keep the booster rule and the front-seat rule apart. To remember: booster exit: belt fit and height; front seat: separate line, under thirteen.

lines.text: Airbags work together with seat belts.

narration.text: Airbags work together with seat belts. An unbelted occupant risks serious injury or death when an airbag deploys. Children under thirteen should never ride in the front seat. So the airbag is not a replacement for the belt; the two work together. For children, the guide's rule is simple: under thirteen, they ride in the back. This rule stands alongside the restraint stages rather than replacing them. To remember: airbags work together with seat belts; unbelted: serious injury or death; under thirteen: never in front.

Here is a quick check: a child is three years old. What kind of seat must the child ride in? Decide before the answer. The child is past the rear-facing stage that runs from birth until age two, and not yet at the booster stage that starts at four. The answer is a car seat with a harness, which may face either rearward or forward. Children aged two to four ride in a harnessed car seat. A helpful hook for this lesson: rear to two, harness to four, booster until the belt fits. In short: children aged two to four must ride in a car seat with a harness, which may face either rearward or forward.

lines.text: Rear to two; harness two to four; booster from four.

narration.text: To sum up, child restraints must meet federal standards and follow both makers' instructions, and a certified technician can check the installation. Keep a child in each stage as long as the seat allows. Rear-facing from birth until two, a harnessed car seat from two to four, then a car or booster seat until the belts fit, usually between eight and twelve. Anyone over four feet nine old enough for a belt wears one. Airbags work with belts, and children under thirteen never ride in front. To remember: approved seats, installed correctly; rear to two; harness two to four; booster from four; under thirteen ride in back.

narration.text: This lesson covers steering. The guide starts with where to hold the wheel, then describes three methods: hand-to-hand steering, hand-over-hand steering and one-hand steering. Each method has its own situations, and the hand positions differ between forward driving and backing. By the end of the lesson you should be able to match a driving situation to the steering method and hand position the guide recommends for it. To remember: hand position; hand-to-hand and hand-over-hand; one-hand steering. A helpful hook for this lesson: hands never cross in hand-to-hand.

lines.text: Outside of the wheel, top half.
Hands at about nine and three.

narration.text: For the best control, hold the outside of the wheel on its top half. Picture the wheel as a clock face, with your hands at about nine and three. Hand-to-hand and hand-over-hand steering can also start from nine and three or ten and two. So the starting point for forward driving is on the upper half of the wheel, at the sides. The twelve o'clock position, at the very top, is a different case that comes up with one-hand steering. To remember: outside of the wheel, top half; picture a clock face; hands at about nine and three.

lines.text: Hands at nine and three or ten and two.
Each hand stays on its own side.
One pulls, one slides; never cross.

narration.text: In hand-to-hand steering, also called pull and push steering, your hands sit at nine and three or ten and two. Each hand stays on its own side of the wheel. One hand pulls while the other slides, and the hands never cross. Hand-to-hand steering never crosses the arms and never lets go of the wheel, so the arms stay out of the airbag area and corrections can be made instantly. To remember: hands at nine and three or ten and two; each hand stays on its own side; one pulls, one slides; never cross. A helpful hook for this lesson: hands never cross in hand-to-hand.

lines.text: Starts from nine and three or ten and two.

narration.text: Hand-over-hand steering also starts from nine and three or ten and two. It is for low-speed turns, limited visibility, intersections, parking and skid recovery. To do it, reach one arm across the other, pull, release the lower hand, and straighten the wheel as the turn ends. So hand-over-hand is the method where the arms do cross, and it belongs to slower, tighter maneuvers like parking and intersection turns. To remember: starts from nine and three or ten and two; low-speed turns, parking, skid recovery; reach across, pull, release, straighten.

lines.text: Trap: one hand at twelve going forward.
Forward: nine and three or ten and two.

narration.text: Here is the trap. One-hand steering with the hand at twelve is recommended only when backing, which differs from the nine and three or ten and two positions used for forward driving. Use one-hand steering when backing up, or when you must reach for controls such as wipers, flashers or lights. The twelve o'clock hand position is recommended only for backing while you turn your body to look behind. Going forward, both hands return to the sides of the wheel. To remember: twelve o'clock: backing only; forward: nine and three or ten and two.

lines.text: What do the hands never do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: in hand-to-hand steering, what must your hands never do? Decide before the answer. In this method, the hands sit at nine and three or ten and two, each on its own side, and one pulls while the other slides. The answer is that the hands never cross. Hand-to-hand steering never crosses the arms and never lets go of the wheel, so the arms stay out of the airbag area and corrections can be made instantly. A helpful hook for this lesson: hands never cross in hand-to-hand. In short: in hand-to-hand steering each hand stays on its own side, one pulls while the other slides, and the hands never cross.

lines.text: Top half, near nine and three.

narration.text: To close, hold the outside of the wheel on its top half with hands at about nine and three. In hand-to-hand steering your hands sit at nine and three or ten and two, each stays on its own side, one pulls while the other slides, and they never cross. Hand-over-hand steering is for low-speed turns, limited visibility, intersections, parking and skid recovery. One-hand steering is for backing or reaching controls, and the twelve o'clock position is only for backing. To remember: top half, near nine and three; hand-to-hand: never cross; hand-over-hand: low speed; twelve: backing.

narration.text: This lesson covers braking and acceleration. The guide names four braking levels and describes the kind of braking to aim for. It explains what an antilock brake system does and does not do, and where to practice hard braking. It finishes with smooth acceleration, which follows the same idea as smooth braking. The key fact to hold onto is what ABS changes and what it leaves the same. To remember: four braking levels; antilock brakes; smooth acceleration. A helpful hook for this lesson: ABS steers, it does not shorten.

The guide names four braking levels: light, medium, firm and emergency. Judging the right pressure is a skill that grows with practice in your vehicle. So braking is not a single action; it is a range, from a light touch to a full emergency stop. Each vehicle responds a little differently, which is why the guide ties the skill to practice in the vehicle you actually drive. To remember: light, medium, firm and emergency; judging pressure grows with practice; practice in your own vehicle. A helpful hook for this lesson: ABS steers, it does not shorten.

lines.text: Aim for light and medium braking.
Brake as if a cup of water sat in your lap.

narration.text: Aim to need only light and medium braking. Brake as if a cup of water sat in your lap. Avoid needless hard stops that could surprise drivers behind you. Smooth acceleration follows the same cup-of-water idea, ranging from simply easing off the brake in stop-and-go traffic to speeding up quickly to avoid a hazard. So the cup of water is the guide's image for both slowing down and speeding up. To remember: aim for light and medium braking; brake as if a cup of water sat in your lap; avoid needless hard stops. A helpful hook for this lesson: ABS steers, it does not shorten.

lines.text: Keep steering in an emergency stop.
The car may shake when it engages.

narration.text: An antilock brake system lets you keep steering during an emergency stop. It does not shorten your stopping distance. You may feel the car shake when it engages. The guide suggests practicing firm or emergency braking in a large open paved area to feel the ABS stop the wheels from locking. So practice in a safe, open space lets you learn what ABS feels like before you need it in traffic. To remember: keep steering in an emergency stop; stopping distance is not shorter; the car may shake when it engages. A helpful hook for this lesson: ABS steers, it does not shorten.

lines.text: Myth: ABS stops the car sooner.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because ABS is a safety feature, many drivers assume it makes the car stop sooner. It does not. An Antilock Brake System lets drivers keep better steering control during emergency braking without shortening stopping distance, and the vehicle may shake slightly when it engages. A car with ABS still needs the same room to stop. Keep your following distance the same whether or not your car has antilock brakes. To remember: ABS keeps steering control; stopping distance stays the same. A helpful hook for this lesson: ABS steers, it does not shorten. In short: the guide names four braking levels and says to aim for light and medium braking, as if a cup of water sat in your lap.

lines.text: What does ABS let you do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: during an emergency stop in a car with antilock brakes, what does ABS let you do? Decide before the answer, and remember the trap. ABS does not shorten your stopping distance. The answer is that it lets you keep steering. An antilock brake system lets you keep steering during an emergency stop, and you may feel the car shake when it engages. A helpful hook for this lesson: ABS steers, it does not shorten. In short: an antilock brake system lets you keep steering during an emergency stop but does not shorten your stopping distance.

lines.text: Cup of water for braking and speed.
ABS steers; it does not shorten.

narration.text: To sum up, the four braking levels are light, medium, firm and emergency, and judging pressure grows with practice in your vehicle. Aim for light and medium braking, brake as if a cup of water sat in your lap, and avoid needless hard stops. ABS lets you keep steering in an emergency stop but does not shorten stopping distance, so practice it in a large open paved area. Accelerate with the same smoothness. To remember: light, medium, firm, emergency; cup of water for braking and speed; ABS steers; it does not shorten.

narration.text: This lesson covers how a vehicle's weight moves while you drive. The guide starts with balance, then names three kinds of weight shift: pitch, roll and yaw. Each one has its own direction, and the questions about them usually turn on that direction. We will go through each shift and then fix the direction of roll in a turn, which is the one learners most often get backward. To remember: balance; pitch, roll and yaw; direction of each shift. A helpful hook for this lesson: pitch front-back, roll side, yaw zig-zag. In short: pitch is the forward and backward weight shift, roll is the side-to-side shift, and yaw is the zig-zag from sharp steering.

lines.text: Weight spread evenly across all tires.

narration.text: Keeping weight evenly spread across all tires keeps the vehicle stable. The guide says this is helped by regular maintenance, correct tire pressure and alignment checks. So stability starts before you drive, with the condition of the vehicle. When the weight is balanced, the vehicle is stable; the weight shifts described next happen when you speed up, slow down or turn. To remember: weight spread evenly across all tires; keeps the vehicle stable; maintenance, tire pressure, alignment. A helpful hook for this lesson: pitch front-back, roll side, yaw zig-zag.

Pitch is the forward and backward weight shift: accelerating loads the rear of the vehicle, while a sudden stop loads the front. Roll is the side-to-side weight shift, and in a left turn centrifugal force pushes the weight onto the outside, or right side, of the vehicle. Yaw is the zig-zag that happens when you steer sharply from side to side, because the front wheels follow the steering while the rear may slide out of line. To remember: pitch: forward and backward; roll: side to side; yaw: the zig-zag. A helpful hook for this lesson: pitch front-back, roll side, yaw zig-zag.

lines.text: Trap: weight moves toward the turn.

narration.text: Here is the trap. In a left turn the weight rolls onto the right, or outside, side of the vehicle, not onto the side you are turning toward. Pitch shifts weight front to back, so acceleration loads the rear and hard braking loads the front, unlike roll, which shifts weight side to side in turns. So in any turn, roll goes to the outside: a left turn puts the weight on the right side. To remember: left turn: weight rolls right; roll goes to the outside. A helpful hook for this lesson: pitch front-back, roll side, yaw zig-zag.

Here is a quick check: you are making a left turn. Which side of the vehicle does the weight roll onto? Decide before the answer, and remember the trap. Roll is the side-to-side shift in a turn. The answer is the right, or outside, side. In a left turn centrifugal force pushes the weight onto the outside, or right side, of the vehicle, not onto the side you are turning toward. A helpful hook for this lesson: pitch front-back, roll side, yaw zig-zag. In short: in a left turn centrifugal force pushes the weight onto the outside, or right side, of the vehicle.

lines.text: Pitch front-back; roll side to side.

narration.text: To close, keeping weight evenly spread across all tires keeps the vehicle stable, helped by maintenance, correct tire pressure and alignment checks. Pitch is the forward and backward shift: accelerating loads the rear and a sudden stop loads the front. Roll is the side-to-side shift, and in a left turn the weight goes onto the outside, or right side. Yaw is the zig-zag that happens when you steer sharply from side to side. To remember: balanced weight, stable vehicle; pitch front-back; roll side to side; yaw is the zig-zag.

narration.text: This lesson covers vehicle reference points, the parts of your own vehicle you use to judge distance. The guide names several, including the left headlight, the center of the hood, the side mirrors and the rear bumper. It gives two specific checks, one using the side mirror and one using the hood center, and both put you a few inches from a line. We will cover what each check tells you. To remember: what reference points are; the side-mirror check; the hood-center check. A helpful hook for this lesson: mirror over the line, front just short.

Vehicle reference points such as the left headlight, the center of the hood, the side mirrors and the rear bumper help you judge distance when parking, turning, backing and stopping. So a reference point is a part of the car you line up with something outside, such as a stop line or a lane marking. Using them lets you place the vehicle accurately even though you cannot see its edges directly from the driver's seat. To remember: left headlight, hood center; side mirrors, rear bumper; parking, turning, backing, stopping.

When the center of your hood lines up with the lane marking, your vehicle is roughly three to six inches from the edge of the lane. So both checks give the same small distance, but they measure different things: one is to the stop line ahead, the other is to the lane edge. The check for the lane edge uses the center of the hood instead. To remember: it is a forward check; front end near the stop line. When the center of your hood lines up with the lane marking, your vehicle is roughly three to six inches from the edge of the lane. A helpful hook for this lesson: mirror over the line, front just short. In short: when the center of your hood lines up with the lane marking, your vehicle is roughly three to six inches from the edge of the lane.

When the stop line appears under your side mirror, your front end is roughly three to six inches from it. When the hood center lines up with the lane marking, your vehicle is roughly three to six inches from the lane edge. lines.text: Areas you cannot see from the seat.
Can hide a car, motorcycle or bicycle.

narration.text: Blind zones are areas you cannot see from the driver's seat. A blind zone can fully hide a car, a motorcyclist or a bicyclist. You are responsible for knowing what is in them. So a blind zone is not an excuse; the guide places the duty on the driver to find out what is there before moving into it. The next slides cover how to shrink your blind zones and how to check them. To remember: areas you cannot see from the seat; can hide a car, motorcycle or bicycle; you are responsible for them. A helpful hook for this lesson: can't see their mirrors? They can't see you.

Shrink blind zones by setting the rearview mirror to see out the back window without stretching, and setting the side mirrors by the traditional or enhanced method. Then still turn your head, with the wheel held straight, to check. A regular scan covers the road ahead, the rearview mirror, both side mirrors and over both shoulders. Recheck and adjust your mirrors every time you get behind the wheel, and keep checking them while you drive. To remember: rearview: back window without stretching; side mirrors: traditional or enhanced; scan ahead, mirrors, both shoulders.

lines.text: Trap: mirrors cover every blind zone.
Keep the wheel straight while you look.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers think well-set mirrors remove blind zones completely. The guide says to set the rearview and side mirrors to shrink blind zones, then still turn your head with the wheel held straight to check. So mirrors make blind zones smaller, but a head check is still part of every lane change. A regular scan includes looking over both shoulders, not only into the mirrors. To remember: still turn your head; keep the wheel straight while you look. A helpful hook for this lesson: can't see their mirrors? They can't see you.

lines.text: Adjust your speed to be seen.
Buses, motor homes, trucks: no zones.
No mirrors visible: you are not seen.

narration.text: Stay out of other drivers' blind zones by adjusting your speed. Take extra care around buses, motor homes and commercial vehicles, whose large blind zones are called no zones. If you cannot see a large vehicle's mirrors, its driver cannot see you. Other drivers' blind zones are handled by speeding up or slowing down until they can see you. So the fix for someone else's blind zone is a change in your speed. To remember: adjust your speed to be seen; buses, motor homes, trucks: no zones; no mirrors visible: you are not seen.

lines.text: You: mirrors, seat, belt, phone, focus.

narration.text: A good pre-drive routine has three parts. Outside the vehicle, check for tire debris, glass, leaks and obstacles such as children or pets. Inside, check for warning lights, clear windows and secured items. Then confirm your mirrors, seat, wheel, belt and a muted phone, and check that you feel healthy, focused and calm. So the routine covers the vehicle, its setup and the driver before every trip. To remember: outside: debris, glass, leaks, obstacles; inside: warning lights, windows, items; you: mirrors, seat, belt, phone, focus.

lines.text: You cannot see a truck's mirrors.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving near a large truck and you cannot see the driver's mirrors. What does that tell you? Decide before the answer. The answer is that the truck's driver cannot see you. If you cannot see a large vehicle's mirrors, its driver cannot see you. Other drivers' blind zones are handled by speeding up or slowing down until they can see you, and large vehicles have the bigger blind zones called no zones. A helpful hook for this lesson: can't see their mirrors? They can't see you. In short: if you cannot see a large vehicle's mirrors, its driver cannot see you, so adjust your speed until they can.

lines.text: Your blind zones are your duty.
Set mirrors, scan, turn your head.
Change speed to be seen; routine first.

narration.text: To close, blind zones can fully hide a car, motorcyclist or bicyclist, and you are responsible for knowing what is in them. Set the rearview and side mirrors to shrink them, still turn your head, and scan the road ahead, mirrors and both shoulders. Stay out of others' blind zones by adjusting speed, take extra care around no zones, and remember that if you cannot see a large vehicle's mirrors its driver cannot see you. Recheck mirrors every drive and run a pre-drive routine. To remember: your blind zones are your duty; set mirrors, scan, turn your head; change speed to be seen; routine first.
